note.note:
History:
• Chief complaint: 1-week history of sore throat followed by dry cough.  
• Timeline  
  – Day 0–1 (Thu/Fri last week): Sore throat began with low-grade fever.  
  – Day 1–2: Dry, non-productive cough started.  
  – Day 3–4: Developed mild exertional shortness of breath, occasional wheeze, and some chest discomfort.  
  – Course has been “up-and-down”; intermittent headaches; fever resolved after first 3 days.  
• Associated symptoms: Reduced appetite, no weight loss, no nasal congestion, no sputum, no haemoptysis, no rash.  
• Triggers/relief: SOB only on exertion (able to walk stairs/exercise); cough not worse at night.  
• Concerns: Patient worried about serious causes (TB, cancer). Requested reassurance, medication advice, and a sick note.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses; explicitly denies asthma or thromboembolic disease.  
• Allergies: Peanuts (no drug allergies).  
• Medications: None (no current prescriptions or OTC noted).  
• Family history: Mother – lung cancer; no familial clotting disorders.  
• Social/other: Non-smoker (occasional past experimentation only), no known asbestos exposure, lives/work in UK >12 yrs, recent travel limited to Europe.  

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation only; no vitals recorded.  
• Patient reports no palpable neck lumps.  
• No other physical findings documented.  
• Mental status: Alert, conversational.  

Impression:
Likely acute viral upper respiratory tract infection / viral bronchitis presenting with dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea.  
DDx consistency:  
1. Viral URI/bronchitis – symptoms and self-limited pattern (highly likely).  
2. COVID-19 infection – compatible but unconfirmed (medium likelihood).  
3. Reactive airway disease triggered by viral infection – possible given wheeze (medium likelihood).  

Management Plan:
• Education & reassurance: Explained benign course; low concern for TB or lung cancer at present.  
• Symptomatic therapy: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for throat discomfort/fever; encourage adequate oral fluids and rest.  
• Administrative: Provided sick note for additional days off work.  
• Safety-netting: Seek in-person medical review if any of the following occur:  
  – Worsening or sudden shortness of breath.  
  – Persisting or worsening symptoms beyond ~4–5 days.  
  – New fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis.  
• Follow-up: Contact GP or urgent care if above red-flags appear or no improvement.  

Patient Summary:
Vincent, reportedly born 09 May 2016 but functioning as a working adult (conflict noted), presents with a 1-week sore throat progressing to dry cough and mild exertional SOB. Features and course are most consistent with a viral respiratory infection; conservative management and short work leave provided with strict return precautions.  

Key Takeaways:
• Take paracetamol as needed, stay well-hydrated, and rest.  
• Expect gradual improvement over the next 4–5 days; if not improving or if breathing worsens, seek face-to-face medical review.  

Next Steps:
• No immediate investigations ordered.  
• Monitor symptoms; consider GP evaluation and possible COVID testing if condition persists or worsens.  
• Review if ongoing wheeze/SOB to assess for possible reactive airway disease.  

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: No vitals, no formal physical exam, no medication reconciliation beyond “none,” no dosing details for paracetamol.  
• Conflicts: Stated DOB (09 May 2016) conflicts with patient description as adult worker.  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor conversational overlaps, no major inaudible sections.
